name: Fatima Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Fatima Hansen, 58, and I've built and repaired power lines for years after a certificate and apprenticeship. I know the salt-damaged fittings on Harbor Road, though I'm paid at the lower end; I like tracing a physical fault, and I use an approved AI assistant every day for photographs and notes after the line is safe.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A burst pipe took nearly all our savings. My partner Nils books freight loads on uneven hours, and our grown children have rent of their own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot the assistant can shorten my report after a repair, but the wire still needs my hands and a meter. I wouldn't call that a new world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like using AI every day, yet our money is already tight. My lower lineworker pay and a burst pipe left less than a month's expenses saved, and Nils's freight-booking hours have been uneven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking my regular line calls and use the approved assistant to sort photos of corroded fittings after each shift. In the first year Nils and I would pause the paid streaming bundle until the pipe bill is cleared; I'd continue checking every tool summary against the signed fault sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious at work and bothered by bills at home. The grown children ask how we're doing, but they're paying their own rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a corroded fitting look like in your photos?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Harbor Road connector gets a green edge where salt reaches the sleeve. I tag the photograph for our crew log. The meter and my eyes settle the repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does Nils's pay vary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Nils books freight loads for a small carrier, and quiet weeks mean shorter shifts. The burst pipe arrived during a quiet week, which is why the account is thin.

say: I'd welcome **shorter repair reports** after a safe field job.
I'd insist **meters and field checks** still govern line repairs.
think: My **lower pay** and burst-pipe bill left less than a month saved.
Nils's **uneven booking shifts** keep the household budget exposed even in a mild scenario.
do: Keep **regular line calls** and sort corroded-fitting photos with the approved assistant.
Pause the **streaming bundle** until the pipe bill clears; check summaries against the signed fault sheet.
feel: **Curious** about tools, bothered by ordinary bills.
S0.quote: The meter and my eyes settle the repair.
fieldNote: Fatima uses **AI daily** for photos and reports but grounds repair decisions in measured voltage and direct inspection.
The **burst-pipe expense** and Nils's variable freight-booking shifts create anxiety before any large AI change.

steps.text: Keep regular paid line calls and inspect Harbor Road connectors
Use the approved assistant to sort completed repair photographs
Pause the streaming bundle until the burst-pipe bill clears

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the carrier and our utility to test planning software with the people who know the routes. Faster dispatch sounds good until a truck follows the wrong feeder and freight goes to the wrong loading bay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My field repairs should continue for now, but Nils spends his day booking loads, which this AI could do cheaply. His hours might shrink soon, and fewer callouts at our depot would make the gap worse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd join the utility's approved route pilot and record every Harbor Road access error for dispatch. In the first year Nils and I would postpone buying a replacement freezer if his booking hours fall, and he'd ask his employer about paid training in warehouse receiving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel interested in the route tool and anxious about Nils. A good map doesn't pay the rent if my partner Nils's freight-booking shift disappears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What access error matters at Harbor Road?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The low gate floods at high tide, while the upper gate has room for the truck. I want the pilot to get that right on a wet evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would receiving work really protect Nils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It might use his knowledge of loads, but I can't promise a receiving post will be open. He would keep booking while asking about the training and actual pay.

say: I'd demand **worker route trials** before planning software changes jobs.
I'd say **correct feeder access** matters more than a neat map.
think: Nils's **freight-booking hours** could fall soon under automated planning at the carrier.
My own **callout income** could shrink if dispatch becomes tighter.
do: Join the **approved route pilot** and log Harbor Road gate errors.
Delay the **freezer replacement** if Nils loses hours; ask about paid receiving training.
feel: **Interested** in the pilot, anxious about Nils's wages.
S1.quote: A good map doesn't pay the rent if my partner Nils's freight-booking shift disappears.
fieldNote: Fatima expects **early household exposure** through Nils's freight booking while her physical repairs continue.
Her **Harbor Road pilot** tests high-tide access, and Nils would ask for paid training without assuming a receiving vacancy.

steps.text: Use the approved route pilot and record high-tide gate errors
Delay replacing the freezer if Nils loses booking hours
Ask Nils’s employer about paid warehouse-receiving training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot thinking AI in 2028 will change Nils's booking desk before robots reach my line work around 2031. We need field trials that show failed repairs and a paid route into inspection.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when a robot can mend a line, and I expect a big reduction in crew hours. Nils may already have lost booking shifts; with less than a month saved and few local utilities, we cannot wait for a perfect job posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask our employee committee for a paid inspection pathway and start collecting verified photos of failures the plans miss. In 2029 I'd enroll if wages continue during training; when robots arrive in 2031 I'd apply for posted inspection jobs here and ask the employment office for help reaching work in the next region.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wake up replaying the two pay packets against the rent. I can learn new equipment, but the queue for paid jobs may be long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a failure photograph show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At Harbor Road, salt hides a cracked sleeve behind a clean outer edge. I'd label the angle and meter reading so a trial report shows more than a pretty image.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a written paid offer that covers travel and rent. Our grown children live nearby, and I wouldn't move both of us on a vendor's forecast.

say: I'd separate **2028 booking AI** from 2031 repair robots.
I'd ask for **failed-repair evidence** and paid inspection training.
think: At **63**, I expect a large reduction in crew hours.
Nils's **booking income** may fall first while our reserve is below one month.
do: Ask the **employee committee** for paid inspection training and log field faults now.
Enroll if **wages continue** in 2029; apply for real inspection jobs and regional travel help in 2031.
feel: **Sleepless** over likely losses in both pay packets.
S2.quote: I can learn new equipment, but the queue for paid jobs may be long.
fieldNote: Fatima expects **major crew-hour loss** by 2031 after possible booking cuts and describes repeated sleepless rent calculations.
Her **photo log** captures a salt-hidden sleeve fault; paid training and a written offer condition her next moves.

steps.text: Ask the employee committee to negotiate paid inspection training
Enroll in inspection training in 2029 if wages continue
Apply for posted inspection jobs when robots arrive
Ask the employment office for travel help to regional interviews

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company five years is enough to trial robots in salt and rain, not just on a clean practice pole. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and repair robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retirement at 66 might work, but Nils's freight income could shrink in 2031 and our savings are nearly gone now. I need a written pension figure before deciding whether to keep climbing or seek another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd request pension estimates for us and share my Harbor Road photo log with the safety group. In 2032 I'd take a paid robot-inspection placement if one opens; in 2034 I'd compare the actual inspection wage with a low-income household budget before choosing work or retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more able to plan than in the fast picture, yet the money is still close. A five-year runway is useful only if the training pays while we take it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would go into the low-income budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, medicines and a quiet freight week, not Nils's best run of bookings. We have no school fees now, but the normal bills still come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who reviews the photo log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The safety group includes field workers and a supervisor. I'd ask them to check the meter readings before they use my photographs as evidence.

say: I'd demand **salt-and-rain trials** before 2034 robots repair lines.
I'd distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from later field robots.
think: Retirement at **66** depends on a written pension and Nils's lower-income case.
Our **near-empty savings** make paid training essential.
do: Request **pension figures** and submit verified Harbor Road photos this year.
Take a **paid inspection placement** if offered in 2032; compare real wages with retirement in 2034.
feel: **More able** to plan, still close to the edge financially.
S3.quote: A five-year runway is useful only if the training pays while we take it.
fieldNote: Fatima's **2034 choice** uses a low freight-income budget because Nils's booking role may change three years earlier.
The **safety group's review** of meter readings keeps her field photographs from becoming unverified claims.

steps.text: Compare written pension figures with rent and a quiet freight week
Submit checked Harbor Road fault photographs to the safety group
Take a paid robot-inspection placement in 2032 if offered
Apply for inspection work in 2034 if retirement income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger workers ten years is enough to record the odd faults that a clean drawing leaves out. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 and field robots around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to have retired from line work before 71, but the burst-pipe debt and Nils's booking wages make that uncertain. If thinking AI takes his desk work in 2036, our retirement budget changes before robots reach my pole work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid field shifts, clear the pipe bill and get written pension statements. In 2037 Nils and I would choose a retirement date only if the low-income budget covers rent; if it doesn't, I'd apply for real inspection work before 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed by the robots and still anxious about money this year. A decade gives us time to adjust, not permission to ignore the pipe bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you save after the pipe bill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move fifteen from each actual extra callout into savings once the pipe is paid. I won't write a monthly amount that depends on overtime the depot hasn't offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your fault record include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Harbor Road sleeve photograph, the salt line and the meter reading, all dated. A new lineworker can check the same spot instead of trusting a clean drawing.

say: I'd ask for **field fault records** during the decade.
I'd note **2039 robots** reach repairs when I'll be 71.
think: Retirement before **71** depends on pension and Nils's booking income.
The **pipe debt** still presses us now, long before robots arrive.
do: Keep **paid field shifts**, clear pipe debt and request pension statements.
Save **fifteen from actual callouts** after debt clears, then review retirement in 2037.
feel: **Less rushed** by robots, still anxious about present bills.
S4.quote: A decade gives us time to adjust, not permission to ignore the pipe bill.
fieldNote: Fatima's **long robot runway** does not settle current debt or Nils's earlier 2036 booking risk.
Her **saving plan** uses real extra callouts only after the pipe bill is cleared, then tests retirement against low income.

steps.text: Keep paid field shifts and clear the burst-pipe bill
Save fifteen from each actual extra callout after debt clears
Set a 2037 retirement date only if low-income figures cover rent
Apply for posted inspection work if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because Nils's booking income could fall before robots cut my repair hours in 2031. Paid inspection training, verified field trials, real jobs and help reaching the next region would give us choices.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the photographs when a robot misses a fault under salt. A beautiful image can leave the dangerous crack out of frame.

headlineQuote: A beautiful image can leave the dangerous crack out of frame.
portrait: Fatima is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a certificate and apprenticeship, low pay and less than one month saved.
A **burst-pipe bill** emptied savings while Nils's uneven freight-booking hours make household income uncertain.
She uses **AI daily** for repair photos and notes but checks each circuit against signed records and meter readings.
The **2031 robot date** alarms her because she expects crew-hour losses after Nils's booking work may shrink.
Longer warning supports **pension checks** from real callouts, but she keeps paid field work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Fatima most because booking AI could cut Nils's income before 2031 robots cut her hours.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid inspection training**, verified field trials, real jobs and regional interview help.
